back: ARM is a family of RISC instruction-set architectures — the 32-bit AArch32 and 64-bit AArch64 execution states — used in Raspberry Pi, smartphones, and virtually all embedded devices, and defined by Arm under license to silicon makers.
An assembler is a tool that turns assembly language (human-readable mnemonics) into machine-code object files the linker can combine.

The **BIOS** (Basic Input/Output System) is the older firmware burned onto the motherboard that runs the moment the power button is pressed, runs a self-test, finds a bootable disk, and hands control to a bootloader.
`bootimage` is a Cargo subcommand (run as `cargo bootimage`) that invokes the `bootloader` crate to turn your Rust kernel ELF into a bootable disk image.
The `bootloader` crate is a Rust library (from *Writing an OS in Rust*) that wraps your freestanding kernel ELF into a bootable disk image so QEMU or real hardware can boot it.
A **bootloader** is a small program that loads your kernel image from disk into memory, sets the CPU into a sane known state, and jumps to your kernel's entry point.
Cargo is Rust's package manager and build tool — the Rust analog of `make` + a dependency manager in one command.
Cosmos (C# Open Source Managed Operating System) is an open-source kit that lets you write an operating system's logic in C#.
A cross-compiler is a compiler that runs on your machine but produces machine code for a *different* CPU (and often a different operating system) than the one it runs on.
ELF (Executable and Linkable Format) is the standard file format for compiled binaries on Unix-like systems — and the format this hub's kernels are built and booted in.
The **entry point** is the symbol — usually `_start` — that the bootloader jumps to when your kernel starts, the first instruction of your kernel that ever runs.
`extern "C"` is a C++ (and Rust, via `#[no_mangle]`/`extern "C"`) language construct that gives a function C linkage so its exported symbol name is not mangled.
**Firmware** is software permanently stored on the motherboard (in ROM/flash) that runs first at power-on and is responsible for starting the machine and finding a bootloader.
A frame allocator is the simplest memory manager: it tracks which fixed-size physical pages (usually 4 KiB each) are free and hands them out one at a time.
A freestanding environment is one where your code assumes no operating system and no standard library exist underneath it — exactly the situation a kernel runs in.
Garbage collection is automatic memory reclamation — and on bare metal it's a burden, because managed runtimes like Go and C# assume an OS underneath to support their collector.
`gccgo` is the Go front-end of the GCC compiler — the only practical way to compile a Go kernel for bare metal in this hub.
The Global Descriptor Table (GDT) is a table of memory-segment descriptors that the CPU consults in protected and long mode to define how memory is laid out and what privileges your code runs with.

**GRUB** (GNU Grand Unified Bootloader) is a free, standard bootloader that loads a Multiboot kernel at 1 MiB, sets up protected mode, and jumps to its entry point — the bootloader this hub's learning path is built on.
Heap allocation is dynamically allocating memory at runtime — and in a kernel, you must implement the allocator yourself, because there's no operating system below to hand out heap memory.
The `hlt` (halt) instruction parks the CPU by stopping execution until an unmasked interrupt arrives to wake it.
A hosted environment is a normal program that assumes an operating system and a standard library (like libc) exist underneath it.
The Interrupt Descriptor Table (IDT) is the kernel's phonebook that tells the CPU where to jump for every one of the 256 possible interrupt numbers (0–255).
IL2CPU is Cosmos OS's original compiler that translates .NET Intermediate Language (IL) into native x86 machine code.
A hardware interrupt is the CPU pausing whatever it is doing to run a registered handler whenever a piece of hardware (like a timer or keyboard) signals that an event has occurred.
An Interrupt Service Routine (ISR) is the handler function the CPU runs for a specific interrupt number after it is dispatched through the [IDT](idt.md).
The kernel is the core program that owns the machine and manages hardware and memory for every other piece of software running on it.
**Limine** is a modern bootloader that supports Multiboot 2 (`0xE85250D6`) and 64-bit kernels, used on the UEFI path where a kernel is booted straight into long mode.
The linker (`ld`) merges all your object files into a single kernel image and places it at a chosen memory address, controlled by a **linker script**.
**Long mode** is the 64-bit CPU mode that modern kernels run in — the mode a UEFI machine boots straight into, giving a kernel 64-bit registers and 64-bit addressing.
Make is a build automation tool that reads a `Makefile` and runs the right compile/link commands whenever files change.
Managed Intermediate Language (IL / CIL) is the platform-neutral bytecode that C# compiles to, which needs a .NET runtime to execute — the reason a C# kernel is fundamentally different.
Memory management is how a kernel keeps track of what RAM exists, what's used, and what's free, and hands it out safely — because, unlike a normal program, there's no OS underneath to do it.
Memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) is when hardware peripherals are controlled by reading from and writing to regular memory addresses, instead of using special I/O instructions.

**Multiboot** is the protocol that lets a standard bootloader load any kernel that follows the rules — a kernel carries a fixed magic header at its very start so a bootloader can find it, validate it, and load it at 1 MiB.
NativeAOT is .NET's ahead-of-time (AOT) compiler that turns managed Intermediate Language (IL) into native machine code — the mechanism Cosmos uses to make a C# kernel bootable.
`#![no_main]` is a Rust crate-level attribute that disables the normal `main()` runtime so you can provide your own kernel entry point.
`#![no_std]` is a Rust crate-level attribute that disables the standard library so the code can run on bare metal with no operating system.
Paging is the CPU feature that translates every *virtual address* your kernel's pointers use into a *physical address* of real RAM, using page tables.
The panic handler is the `#[panic_handler]` function that runs when a Rust kernel panics — and since there is no OS to report the error to, the kernel must define this itself.
Physical memory is the actual RAM installed in the machine, while virtual memory is the address space your code sees after the CPU's paging feature translates it.
The PIC (Programmable Interrupt Controller) and its modern replacement the APIC are the chips that route hardware interrupt signals (timer, keyboard) from devices to the CPU.
**Protected mode** is the 32-bit CPU mode with memory protection and privilege levels that Multiboot v1 loads kernels into — the mode most x86 "bare bones" kernels actually run in.
QEMU is a free, open-source emulator that runs your kernel like a real PC on your desktop — safely and instantly.
**Real mode** is the 16-bit CPU mode the x86 starts in at power-on, with no memory protection and direct access to hardware — the mode every BIOS-path boot chain begins in.

RISC-V is an open, free, modular RISC instruction-set architecture (ISA) defined by the RISC-V International spec, with base integer ISAs (RV32/RV64/RV128) plus standard extensions such as I/M/A/F/D/C.
`rustup` is Rust's toolchain manager — it installs, switches, and pins Rust toolchains and their targets, which is essential for bare-metal cross-compilation.
A system call (syscall) is the controlled way a user-space program asks the kernel to perform a privileged service for it, rather than touching hardware or kernel memory directly.
The text-mode cursor is the blinking position indicator in the VGA text buffer that marks where the next character will be written.

**UEFI** (Unified Extensible Firmware Interface) is the modern replacement for BIOS — motherboard firmware that is 64-bit native, boots the CPU directly into long mode, and hands control to a bootloader.
The VGA framebuffer is the fixed block of memory at `0xB8000` where the VGA text screen lives: each character on the 80×25 screen is one 2-byte cell stored here.
VGA text mode is the basic 80×25 character display mode a minimal kernel writes to by placing 2-byte cells directly in memory at `0xB8000`.
x86 is the CPU architecture family — 32-bit (`i686`) and 64-bit (`x86_64`) — that every kernel in this hub targets.
